The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to launch a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance (the GCP equivalent of an AWS EC2 instance) that is equipped with an **NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU** and runs **Ubuntu 20.04 LTS**.

> **Prerequisites**  
> 1. You have a Google Cloud project with billing enabled.  
> 2. The **Compute Engine API** is enabled for that project.  
> 3. You have the **gcloud CLI** installed and authenticated (`gcloud auth login`).  
> 4. You have the **GPU quota** for the zone you plan to use (e.g., `nvidia-a6000` in `us-central1-a`).  
> 5. You have the **NVIDIA GPU driver** installed on the instance after it boots (see the “Driver install” section below).

---

## 1. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Variables – replace with your own values
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"          # pick a zone that supports RTX A6000
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8" # 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM – adjust as needed
GPU_COUNT=1
GPU_TYPE="nvidia-a6000"
IMAGE_FAMILY="ubuntu-2004-lts"
IMAGE_PROJECT="ubuntu-os-cloud"

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  --machine-type="$MACHINE_TYPE" \
  --accelerator="type=$GPU_TYPE,count=$GPU_COUNT" \
  --image-family="$IMAGE_FAMILY" \
  --image-project="$IMAGE_PROJECT" \
  --boot-disk-size=100GB \
  --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
  --tags=http-server,https-server \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
```

### What the command does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU & RAM configuration |
| `--accelerator` | Adds the GPU (type + count) |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Boots from the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| `--boot-disk-size` | Size of the root disk |
| `--boot-disk-type` | SSD for better I/O |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh` | Optional script that runs on first boot (see below) |
| `--tags` | Enables HTTP/HTTPS firewall rules if you need them |
| `--scopes` | Grants the instance full Cloud Platform access (adjust if you want tighter scopes) |

---

## 2. Using the REST API (JSON body)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine REST API directly (e.g., from a custom application), here’s the exact JSON payload you would POST to:

```http
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/instances
Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-ubuntu",
  "machineType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "accelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-a6000",
      "acceleratorCount": 1
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\nsudo apt-get update\nsudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-535\n"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  }
}
```

> **Note**: Replace `{PROJECT_ID}` and `{ZONE}` with your actual project ID and zone.  
> The `accessToken` must be a valid OAuth 2.0 token with the `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` scope.

---

## 3. Installing the NVIDIA GPU Driver

Google Cloud does **not** install GPU drivers automatically.  
You can either:

1. **Use the startup script** (as shown above) to install the driver on boot.  
   ```bash
   # startup.sh
   #!/bin/bash
   sudo apt-get update
   sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-535
   sudo reboot
   ```

2. **Manually SSH into the instance** after it boots and run:
   ```bash
   sudo apt-get update
   sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-535
   ```

> The driver version (`535` in the example) may change; check the [official NVIDIA driver list](https://www.nvidia.com/Download/index.aspx) for the latest supported version on Ubuntu 20.04.

---

## 4. Verifying the GPU

After the instance is running and the driver is installed, SSH into it:

```bash
gcloud compute ssh rtx-a6000-ubuntu --project="$PROJECT_ID" --zone="$ZONE"
```

Then run:

```bash
nvidia-smi
```

You should see output similar to:

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 535.54.03    Driver Version: 535.54.03    CUDA Version: 12.2     |
|-------------------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| GPU  Name        Persistence-M| Bus-Id        Disp.A | Volatile Uncorr. ECC |
| Fan  Temp  Perf  Pwr:Usage/Cap|         Memory-Usage | GPU-Util  Compute M. |
|                               |                      |               MIG M. |
|===============================+======================+======================|
|   0  NVIDIA RTX A6000     Off | 00000000:01:00.0 Off |                  N/A |
|  0%   35C    P8    15W / 300W |      0MiB / 24576MiB |      0%      Default |
+-------------------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
```

---

## 5. Cleaning Up

When you’re done, delete the instance to avoid incurring charges:

```bash
gcloud compute instances delete rtx-a6000-ubuntu \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  --quiet
```

---

### Quick Reference

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `gcloud compute instances create …` | Create instance via CLI |
| `POST /compute/v1/projects/.../zones/.../instances` | Create instance via REST |
| `nvidia-smi` | Verify GPU presence |
| `gcloud compute instances delete …` | Delete instance |

Feel free to copy/paste the snippets into your terminal or scripts. If you hit any quota limits or need a different machine type, just adjust the `--machine-type` and `--accelerator` values accordingly. Happy GPU computing!
